newsitem.title: FRANCE: Minicar segment gleams with Mercedes.
newsitem.headline: Minicar segment gleams with Mercedes.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz is the last name one expects to find in the inexpensive minicar segment, but the prestigious German manufacturer has swerved off course with a tiny model which will be shown in Paris next week.

Ford Motor Co. will also display a new minicar at the Paris car show, the Ka. Renault SA will show off a revamped version of its trend-setting Twingo, and Suzuki will introduce the lightweight (1,600-pound) Alto.
Mercedes' debut in the so-called A class reflects a renewed interest in minicars among automakers, who previously treated the segment as a niche for first-time owners with little money.
Minicars are among the least profitable vehicles, both in terms of profit margins and volumes -- around 600,000 are sold each year in Europe, compared with 3.3 million small cars.

But manufacturers expect minicar sales in Europe to double or even triple over the next five years, and many are counting on demand for richly appointed, option-packed versions from a new breed of customers.
"If you look at the demographics in Europe, people are getting older and environmentally sensitive," said analyst Arthur Maher at consulting firm DRI McGraw Hill.
"Cities are more congested. More households have two or three vehicles and they're not looking for something cheap, but rather something affordable, for town travel," he said.
He expects minicar prices to overlap with prices of small cars, which tend to have slightly different characteristics but do not necessarily attract a wealthier customer.
"The market in Europe is not growing very fast, but it is becoming more fragmented. It's more a question of people switching from one niche to another," he said.
Daimler Benz, which owns Mercedes, has linked up with Swiss Swatchmaker SMH to build the Smart minicar by 1998, and there is talk of Volkswagen turning out a mini Polo.

But the headlong rush to produce tiny cars is not without risk, and Maher worries about automakers' expectations. He said their minicar production plans assume a market of 1.6 million sales annually within five years, whereas he expects sales over that period to grow to only around 1.2 million a year.
